ety.text: First attested in 1800. From French isolation, from isolé, placed on an island (thus away from other people). Equivalent to isolate + -ion.

senses.d: The state of being isolated, detached, or separated; the state of being away from other people.
ex: She lived her final year in complete isolation, not wanting to see anybody.

senses.d: The act of isolating.
The state of not having diplomatic relations with other countries (either with most or all other countries, or with specified other countries).
The obtaining of an element from one of its compounds, or of a compound from a mixture
The separation of a patient, suffering from a contagious disease, from contact with others (compare: quarantine)
ex: Upon returning from the field, he went into isolation for a week so as not to infect anyone with potential diseases.

senses.d: A database property that determines when and how changes made in one transaction are visible to other concurrent transactions.
A Freudian defense mechanism in which a person suppresses a harmful thought from developing into a train of thought.

grp.label: diplomacy: state of not having diplomatic relations
chemistry: separation of a component from a mixture
medicine: separation of a patient from others

ety.text: From isoler + -ment, first attested in 1701.
From isolare + -mento.
From aislar + -miento.
Inherited from Latin sōlitātem. Doublet of saudade, which was borrowed from Portuguese.

senses.d: To set apart or cut off from others.
To place in quarantine or isolation.
To separate a substance in pure form from a mixture.
To insulate, or make free of external influence.
To separate a pure strain of bacteria etc. from a mixed culture.
To insulate an electrical component from a source of electricity.
To self-isolate.
Something that has been isolated.
ex: We used electropherotypes in order to differentiate the original parental strains or isolates from the finally tumor cell-adapted isolates.

senses.d: isolated.
